C1SZgQ0fWY8.title: How You Influence 100s of People You'll Never Meet
C1SZgQ0fWY8.text: So I want to talk to you about: is there a theme when people realize, hey, I want to live differently. So let me tell you a story about resistance during the Second World War. I grew up in the Netherlands and I was always obsessed as a young boy why so few people joined the resistance during the Second World War. So the Netherlands was actually the country where the highest percentage of Jewish citizens were taken away and murdered in gas chambers. More than 80% of the entire Jewish population was taken away. And most people, most Dutch people didn't do much. It's not that they liked the Nazis. Most people didn't like the Nazis, but they were like, "What can I do?" And we don't really know what's happening to them, and well, it's perhaps risky. So as a young boy I was always obsessed with that question: what would I have done? And for many years I assumed that there must be something like the heroic personality, right? It turns out that after the war there were a few big research projects for which hundreds and hundreds of resistance heroes were interviewed. Now what the researchers discovered is that there's basically nothing. And so this was really a cross-section of the population, people from the left to the right, rich, poor, young, old, men, women, professors, plumbers, could be anything. It was only in the mid '90s that another group of researchers looked at the data again and said, "Hey, wait a minute. There is actually one variable that explains this heroic behavior really well." And the title of that paper is the importance of being asked, because it turns out that in 96% of all cases when people were asked to join the resistance they said yes. Now they weren't asked to immediately hide persecuted Jews in their cellars. It often starts with a small ask like, hey, can you help distributing these illegal newspapers? Right? And then things start escalating and people are often surprised by what can happen to them and the kind of person that they can become. There is also, interestingly enough, an almost self aspect here. People at some point want to be proud of themselves, right? They start seeing themselves in a different way. It's like a virus that is spreading. And this, by the way, explains why resistance during the Second World War in the Netherlands and other countries was not evenly spread out over the country. That's what you would expect if it was a personality trait. No, it was a highly local phenomenon. It spread like a virus, right? And you also had, admittedly, a few super spreaders, people who just asked a lot of people to join the movement. We need a word that's like virus but good. Like, as individuals. Exactly. Culturally it does happen. There are ideas that actually strengthen us and it's like the opposite of a virus. That's such a good point. So Nicholas Christakis is an incredible researcher in the US. He's done a lot of research into social contagion and also the contagion of goodness. Here's one experiment. People played kind of an economic game. They were given a little bit of cash and then at some point they face the choice about how generous they would be. Now what the experiments did is they randomly asked a few players who were in secret to be more generous to some people than to others. Now then the people would go on to play a second round of the same game and a third round of the same game but always with different people. You know what's so interesting is that the people who in the first round were playing the game with someone who was really generous, they became more generous in the second round and they influenced people in that second round, and then even those people who had never met the people in the first round also started to become more generous. So then people in the third and the fourth round were more generous because of the actions of someone in the first round that they had never met. Right? And that is, I think, such a beautiful metaphor for thinking about social behavior. Our behavior is insanely contagious. We are continuously throwing pebbles in the pond and every single day we are influencing dozens, maybe even hundreds of people that we never even meet.

T_4JA0qj8aE.title: Do Rich People Wear Jackets?
T_4JA0qj8aE.text: We had a rich coordinator, like a rich consultant on set who helped tell us what rich people would do. Are you serious? Yeah. That is hilarious. Well, I'll tell you a couple of things. One of them is a famous one that was in a bunch of interviews. Just so you know, the rich don't have big hefty thick jackets, because when they're in the winter, they're not going to be outside that long. Don't worry about it. They don't really have to worry about coats. Or I'll give you another one: when you're entering a helicopter, we normal people duck our heads because we think the blades are going to chop our head off, and then they're like, never, no one, you've been going on helicopters for years, so you could see some of us walking to helicopters, we're like, not going to lower my head. [laughter]
